title: A Boston Grad, a Dead Cockroach and a 40-Day March. India's Exam Revolt Just Went Mainstream.
excerpt: The Cockroach Janta Party started as a meme. Now CNN is at the protest site, Congress is backing a nationwide campaign, and the government is calling students terrorists.
body:
What began as a satirical insult — calling India's unemployed young people "cockroaches" — has mutated into the most organised youth-led political movement the country has seen in a decade. And in the past week, it has crossed a threshold that neither the ruling BJP nor the opposition expected.

On Saturday, CNN filed a feature from the protest encampment at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, where Abhijeet Dipke, the 30-year-old Boston University graduate who founded the Cockroach Janta Party, has been camped out since June 20. "We are here for the long haul, no matter how many days it takes," Dipke told the network, as crowds swelled to roughly 500 by evening. "We are going to be here until Dharmendra Pradhan resigns."

The name is a taunt. The Cockroach Janta Party — CJP — riffs on the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. Its mascot, a cockroach, was adopted after India's chief justice made comments that were widely interpreted as comparing the country's jobless youth to the insect. Its target is specific: the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the 2026 NEET paper leak, the second such scandal in two years.

## Two Million Students, One Broken Exam

The National Eligibility cum Entrance Test is the single gateway to medical education in India. About 2.3 million students sat for it in May. The paper was leaked. The exam was scrapped. A re-sit was held on June 21, with question papers airlifted by Indian Air Force aircraft to more than 5,000 test centres — a logistical operation that itself underscored how broken the system had become.

Authorities also blocked Telegram for 150 million Indian users to disrupt exam-fraud channels on the platform, a move the Delhi High Court later upheld. The re-sit went off without incident, but the answer key released this week has triggered fresh objections, with candidates reporting discrepancies.

For students who spent years in cramming centres, gave up social lives, and bet their families' savings on a single test, the pattern is devastating. "You did your best and the whole procedure failed," Muskan Choudhary, a 20-year-old in Rajasthan who took the exam for the fourth time, told The Wall Street Journal.

## Congress Smells an Opening

On Thursday, Congress announced a 40-day nationwide campaign titled 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' — Voice of Students — demanding Pradhan's resignation and a full overhaul of India's examination system. The campaign, launching on June 30, will cover 28 cities with leaflet drives, campus outreach and street-corner meetings, culminating in a "Delhi Chalo" march on August 9.

"They talk about running a country of 130 crore people, but they cannot even conduct an examination properly for 23 lakh students," Congress leader Satej Patil said. "The confidence students had that they would get marks based on what they studied is gone. That trust has been shattered."

It is the first time a mainstream opposition party has formally hitched its wagon to the youth anger that the CJP channelled. The move signals that the NEET controversy is no longer a student grievance — it is a political fault line heading into state assembly elections later this year.

## The Government Pushes Back — Hard

The BJP has not taken the challenge lightly. Education Minister Pradhan accused the CJP of undermining democratic processes and referred to the movement as the "B-team of terror groups" in an interview with NDTV. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology ordered CJP's X account blocked in India under national-security provisions within a week of its formation, when it had 90,000 followers. Dipke challenged the block in the Delhi High Court. Minutes after the takedown, the party re-emerged under a new handle: "Cockroach is Back."

The Supreme Court, meanwhile, has sought a status report on the implementation of reforms recommended after the 2024 NEET leak — a signal that the judiciary is watching.

## Why the Diaspora Is Watching

For NRI families, the exam crisis strikes close to home. Many parents who built careers abroad did so partly because India's education system rewarded merit. If the entrance exam itself is compromised — leaked, scrapped and re-run under military guard — the implicit promise that hard work will be fairly rewarded no longer holds. Students who might have stayed in India for medical school are now looking at seats in the Caribbean, Eastern Europe and the Philippines.

Dipke himself embodies the loop: an Indian who went to Boston, came back, and is now trying to fix the system from the inside. "It has only been a month since we started, and less than two weeks since I returned to India," he told CNN. "We are going to make a statement."

The 40-day campaign starts on Monday. The Delhi march is set for August 9 — the anniversary of the Quit India movement. Whether the symbolism translates into political pressure will depend on whether India's Gen Z can sustain what they started with a meme and a dead cockroach.
